items.question: Why do you see the human form factor as a compelling choice for robots doing factory work?
items.object: The human form factor in robotics
items.answer: You know, I think that we're really a species of workarounds in everything that we do. We have workarounds. We have shortcuts. We have ways that don't really fit the way that we're supposed to do things, but that's how they get done. That's part of becoming an adult: realizing that the org chart doesn't represent the full view of relationships, right? And so, as you look at all of these workarounds, you do have all kinds of things that just need to be, you know, through a factory, that need to be carried somewhere that you didn't think that they did. Parts that need to be discarded, things that they need to adapt. And as you really start looking at that, you need dexterity and locomotion to do it. And so there are a lot of things you could think about, what form factors could fit, but the only form factor that we know fits all of these jobs is the human form factor, because humans are doing it today. And so, to everyone who wonders about the human form factor, and I always did, I would turn them to the question of why do we still have so many humans in all of these factories, right? I walk into them and they are packed with robots, right? There are all kinds of AB and FIC and industrial robots, but there are also human beings everywhere. And so, that's always my first question when I walk in: what are all these people doing here? And that's what we'll spend the next couple hours as we tour any facility talking about: why are they still humans?

items.question: What do you appreciate about the human form factor when you think about designing robots?
items.object: The human form factor as a design for robots
items.answer: Well, the human hand is incredible. So that's a big portion of it. I think about that every time I'm balancing a mug of coffee as I carry in groceries and have a kid in my arm, right? And I'm still able to open the door. The human form factor is pretty amazing for things like that. But it also is being bipedal and being able to move around all these spaces, being able to sidestep, move forward and backwards, without taking up a lot of room that wheels might or that a base might. And then also the human judgment, right? When you put all those things together, you start to really get an appreciation of the human design. You start to learn a lot about the eyes when you're going into perception. You start looking a lot at the mouth when you have the robot have speakers. All these things are actually designed very well.

items.question: How do you evaluate dexterity and strength when choosing a robotic hand?
items.object: Dexterity and strength in robotic hand design
items.answer: Well, there are two questions about the hands, I think. One is how dextrous are they? So how small of an object, how thin of an object can they pick up? Can they pick up a pin? Can they do electrical wires? Things like that. The other is in strength. And so, how much can they lift? For how long can they lift it? Can they pull these things up? How much torque can they produce? And so, when you're really looking at dexterity and strength, I think that there are ways to have actuators in the hand that have lots of dexterity. And I think if that's the hand that I'm thinking of, it's an incredible one. Watched it all over YouTube and immediately went to my hand team and I said, "Why aren't we using this?" And they wrote back, "Strength."

items.question: How do you think about hand-design trade-offs for humanoid robots intended for business and defense?
items.object: Hand-design trade-offs for humanoid robots serving business and defense
items.answer: I think right now, as we're seeing it, there are so many humanoid companies. It's a horse race for all this. And you have to really think about where you want to land in that market. We are fully dedicated to businesses and defense. That's what we're making our robots for. Most other people are making it for the homes and business. But when you're making those kind of design trade-offs and you're looking to fold a lot of clothes and do laundry, you're looking to empty a dishwasher, all those things don't require that much strength. And so when you're looking at defense use cases, when you're looking at industrial use cases, you want as much strength as possible. And so I think for us, that's why we've still kept things in the forearm. But these are all the kind of choices we're out there with customers. We bring back all of their pieces. You'll see all these things because that's what we test on. That's the standard that we need to get to.

items.question: How do you see the current state of humanoid robot development?
items.object: The state of humanoid robot development
items.answer: I think most of the companies are there. There are a couple breakouts. There's Physical Intelligence, there's Skild, that are both really just working on the brain. I think all the ones that were just working hardware seem to be getting scooped up. But we'll see. I think that really this is one of those problems where the humanoid is a lot more figured out than I thought before I got into this. And as I've gone around and seen everybody else's robots, and you go to Germany and DLR, they're kind of NASA over there, and looked at their humanoid, you really start to see all the parts are the same, right? But for everybody else, the hardware isn't—you kind of know how to place it together and everybody needs to solve hands. Everybody's facing the same challenges right now.

items.question: How do you think about the balance between making humanoid robot parts in house and buying them from suppliers?
items.object: In-house manufacturing versus suppliers for humanoid robots
items.answer: We're building a lot of bespoke parts in house. We have CNC machines. A lot of this, especially for me doing the second time around with lots of manufacturing in the past, you start to think that your suppliers are these big vendors that make all this great stuff and you could never touch their business. And then you go visit them and you find three guys in a storage unit somewhere, hooked up to a generator, and you're going, "Is this what I've been paid? No wonder I can't scale," right? And so you kind of end up taking those things in house. And we've done a lot of that this time around, really saying, what is a part that we can make? How can we get as close to just taking things from nature and turning it into this robot? But with that, you are still going to have a steering wheel, you're still going to have tires, you're still going to have all the basic parts, right? But some people are going to be building Ferraris and some people are going to be building Honda Civics.

items.question: Why do you see building your own humanoid robot actuators from scratch as an important differentiator?
items.object: Building humanoid robot actuators in house
items.answer: And we are building ours from scratch. Our actuators, yes. And our actuators are really our differentiator, I think, because you do realize anybody that's breaking down a humanoid robot, almost all the cost is in the actuators. And that's where almost all of the speed comes from. That's where a lot of the problems are going to come from. So, it's one of these critical parts, right? The hand needs to be—you need to get the hand right so that you can do all the skills, but you need to get the actuators right so that it doesn't break down all the time, that it can actually make economic sense, all these things. items.answer: And so, throughout defense, we're the only company that's selling humanoids to Department of Defense. And so, you go where the case leads you, right? You have some people that are looking at logistics, like motor transportation, fixing trucks, aviation, doing all of this maintenance, refueling things like that to aircraft. But you also have people that are interested in the kinetic side, really protecting soldiers, and that is just like you mentioned: putting a charge on a door, being able to blow that up, being able to carry out dead bodies off of the battlefield—a very dangerous task a lot of people do—being the point man in a patrol. items.question: How do you understand the advantage of latent space variable analysis for controlling a robot?
items.object: Latent space variable analysis for robot control
items.answer: Specifically, latent space variable analysis is what we're doing, which ultimately means you're understanding the relationships between objects. You're understanding the physics of what's happening through these videos. So rather than having to mimic any direct movement, like a teleoperator would remember all the different ways that I grasp a cup, this actually understands the relationships between all of these things and then can make decisions about how it should go about interacting with the world.

items.question: How do you think about the challenge of training robots to understand and interact with the physical world?
items.object: Training robots to understand and interact with the physical world
items.answer: So it's really interesting. Everybody saw ChatGPT, and all these companies now, Perplexity and OpenAI and all these, are all using large language models, and those are all working. We just threw a ton of compute at it, and we had all of this language already out there, right? So it's able to pull from this huge corpus of language that we have on the internet, but we don't have all that kind of real-world data. So there's big dearth in actually just picking up cups and things like that. We do have videos, but we don't know if they're close enough, if they're at the right angles, if there's a way to use—I don't know if there's a way to use Seinfeld reruns and be able to train a robot, but we haven't figured that out yet. So instead, people have to turn to either doing this in simulation. They just have to build a robot like a video game and try to train it there and then see how that comes on there. That's a very good way to do it, except that it's very tough to overcome the gap between the simulation and reality when the robot actually does it. The second would be teleoperating. So that's where you always see these people with VR goggles on and the gloves, and they're trying to control these things. You can train it to just do that over and over again and the robot will soon learn, "Okay, that's how I go there." And the other way would be video. And so for us, it is video. It's first-person video and third-person video. So we'll have someone wear a GoPro. We'll have them wear either chest cam or we've got two that go on a helmet. And then we've got other ones that are sitting on tripods outside of them to show the larger action they're working with them. And I think as I've gotten more involved with the AI and looking at what our AI team does, it looks to me like these are all—it's not really you choose one. Everybody is using all of them, but it depends on the chef, how much they use of each ingredient. And so I think we're pretty heavy on videos and what we're putting into these. But what that ultimately creates is a robot that can understand and interact with the world with the task that we fed into it.

items.question: How do you see training robots on specific tasks leading to a generalizable robot model?
items.object: Foundation Future Industries’ approach to generalizable robot models
items.answer: So ultimately, as we train all of these different robots to do these tasks, they'll all be out there collecting all this different data that we will turn into a generalizable model. I think this was true six months ago. I think it's still true today. We're the only ones that are sort of taking the approach that Tesla took on cars, and that includes Tesla on Optimus. Tesla, I think, is brute-forcing a lot of teleoperating. But the way that they did it with cars was they just had people drive and the car would collect all of that data of exactly what was happening in the camera and exactly what the driver did. By doing that enough, it was able to create a model that would work, be able to navigate the world. And so I think for us right now, we're picking very similar tasks to each other, but there are lots of differences that come in in the real world of pulling those things off. And so as we collect up all that data, that will feed into a generalizable model.

items.question: How do you think about handling unexpected situations when deploying robots to perform specific tasks in the real world?
items.object: Handling unexpected situations in early robot deployments
items.answer: So it's been really interesting as we've broken down these tasks, because in almost everything we've done there's the base case and then there are contingencies. Contingencies have a very long tail but don't pop up that often. And so there's some ability to use humans and training side by side to have humans handle whatever that situation is. Whenever a robot's out there, for example, it will be out there with Marines, right? They can go and handle some of these situations. But that's again where we're finding contingencies are long, but the probability of them is not as infinite as you would think. But everybody knows the videos of a Tesla that is driving, somebody's been sleeping in their car and there's a tree in the road and it crashes into that, because that was just a tiny chance of that happening. Those things are going to happen. That's largely going to be the case in these early models. We deal with them. But it's amazing how many contingencies you can really plan for and how much video data you can collect to make up for them.

items.question: How do you think about the risk of losing robots sent to perform exposed tasks on the battlefield in Ukraine?

items.question: Why do you believe humanoid robots will work far sooner than most people expect?

And so I went through the archives and found, in I think it's 1906, October 1906, there is an article that says why there will never be heavier-than-air flight. It says so many people have been trying planes, and the analogy that it uses, the math that it does, says, "If you look at how long it took birds to evolve, you would already have almost a million years. These are going to be working far sooner than anybody thinks, and people are going to be shocked at the change that it makes in the world.

items.question: Does the prospect of humanoid robots replacing factory workers concern you?
items.object: Humanoid robots replacing factory workers
items.answer: No, not in the least. I really look at these tasks and you'll watch these people. I'll sit up. They have little ladders that you can climb up, and I'll sit there and watch them for hours. I'll be looking across the factory and watching these people pick up a piece of plastic, hold it under camera, put on a label, put it in packaging. And I think all of these humans have stolen robot jobs. These were all stolen from robots and we're taking them back. Nobody wants to go to work. We hang with all these people. My wife will come on site. She brings all these fancy Starbucks drinks for everybody and we walk around. We talk with everybody in there. I don't know anybody in the plants that we're operating in that is upset that the robot has taken a job. It's just the same as a Fanuc robot coming in and doing something. Our most frequently asked question, I always say, is, "Can I take a selfie with it?" The people love to come up. They love to say we're working with humanoids. And I think overall the best example is really ATMs. When the ATM came out, people said, "This is going to put bank tellers out of business." But sure enough, it actually just meant that we expanded the number of banks to the point that we have more bank tellers today than we ever did before the ATM. So, with any technology right now, we're replacing a lot of jobs, but then I think very quickly people see they can expand because they have this technology. They go, "We can start a new plant." And so where all of that goes, I'm very optimistic about how many jobs that's going to create, how many human beings still need to be involved in those processes, and how cool the work is that they're going to be doing because it's very fun working with robots.

items.question: Why do you think Foundation Future Industries has been able to deploy robots on full contracts faster than other companies?
items.object: Foundation Future Industries’ approach to deploying robots on full contracts
items.answer: I think the reason that we've been able to deploy more, and on full contracts, not pilots and these little tests, comes down more to solving the whole problem. In startups I see this all the time: they kind of go in and handle just some base case, but they can't make an economic case. There was a robot a couple years ago that was dipping fries into a deep fryer and taking them out, and they were saying, "We're going to replace the fry cook," but they couldn't open the bag of fries, right? That just encapsulates everything that people do wrong in their go-to-market strategy. And so it's interesting, when you go back and look at Edison, the most important part of what Edison did, I think, was that there were already light bulbs around, and electricity's always been around. He didn't invent electricity, right? But he realized you needed to have a power plant and that you were going to need to do that for all the homes around. And so he solved the whole product. He was able to put it out there and then made the innovations to make it cheap enough that it was worth people getting. It's those kinds of human and economic conditions that you really need to satisfy. And that's why I think we've figured out a way to get these robots into action a lot sooner than anybody else has: really just looking at the whole product, putting ourselves in the customer's shoes, and saying, "What am I paying today? How robust does this robot need to be for me to really trust that this robot can do my part?" And that's been the real innovation that we've figured out to get these robots out faster.

items.question: How do you understand the challenge of selling to the military compared with selling to a large business?

items.answer: It's hard to sell things to a business. And the reason that there is a lot of red tape in a lot of these places, but the real problem is there aren't full decision makers that can simply say, "That's going there," and nobody's going to say anything about it. Every decision that they make is political. And so you have to build coalitions. You have to get a large tent if you want to put these things out there. And I think the military is largely the same. We've talked a lot with Congress about this. We've talked a lot with generals about this. We've talked a lot with soldiers on the line.
